I turned my social life into a MotoGP and F1 championship. Yes, with standings, race results and records 🏁

Meet PADGP (Putu Agas Darmawa: Grand Prix), a personal project I built solo, frontend and backend, in my free time. I wanted a place to document my emotional journey, my friendships, and the history of my social life, then I found the right language for it in motorsport. I'm obsessed with MotoGP and F1, so I built this app with both style and logic to track it all.

How it works then? Roughly every two weeks counts as a "race", modelled on a MotoGP weekend. I look back at that period and rank the people in my life by how close we were, based on depth, consistency, trust and memorable moments. Points follow the real MotoGP points system (25 for a win, down to 1 for 15th), and whoever tops the season is World Champion. The "riders" are real people from different chapters of my life.

The video shows one feature: rider standings. Standings are calculated from race results, and the champion is only crowned once the title is mathematically clinched, just like the real championships. I recreated the graphic from the real MotoGP and F1 broadcasts, and you can switch between a MotoGP style and an F1 style. You'll also see the original broadcast graphics I used as references, and my GitHub repos in the video.

By the way, this is the 4th version of PADGP: Vue in 2021, Svelte in 2023, then two versions in React (Next.js): v1 in 2024-2025 and v2 in 2026. For v2, I started from scratch in August 2026 and brought in what I learned from two places. Gemini API and TanStack Query came from a project I built for Google's JuaraVibeCoding event in May 2026. From my remote freelance frontend job for a company in Jakarta (2025-2026), I brought in Backend For Frontend, git branching, and loading states for data fetching.

The git part is the biggest change. In every previous version, I committed straight to main, which I now know is a bad habit. This is the first PADGP where I use a branch per feature. The end of the video has the proof 😄

Built with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, TanStack Query, Supabase, GSAP and shadcn. Beyond standings, the app also has records tracking, rider statistics, head-to-head rider comparison, and more. Gemini turns each rider's data into a bio written like professional journalism.

The app and repo are private for now because it still uses real photos of my friends. I'll make it public once it's finished and the real photos are replaced with dummy ones.

Design references are in the first comment.

Note: This is not affiliated with MotoGP or F1. Team logos belong to their respective owners, and the MotoGP/F1 branding in the video is recreated for the design exercise.

This is the first post in a series where I'll document the features of PADGP that I built using MotoGP and F1 as references. Stay tuned! 👀

USTR'S NEW TARIFF PROPOSALS. WHAT LIFESTYLE BRANDS NEED TO KNOW.

Your sourcing map just got redrawn, and the clock is already running.

Today the U.S. Trade Representative wrapped up its Section 301 investigations into "structural excess capacity" and found that the trade practices of 14 economies hurt U.S. commerce. 

It has now proposed new tariffs on all of them. 

None of this is final yet. 

But for anyone sourcing apparel, footwear or home goods overseas, this is the moment to start planning.

WHO GETS HIT HARDEST

Vietnam has the highest proposed rate, up to 35%, and textiles, apparel and footwear are named directly. India could see up to 25%, and China up to 20% on most goods. Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia are all looking at 18%, with Bangladesh's garment sector and Cambodia's and Indonesia's apparel industries called out by name. The EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland sit at 15%.

THE FINE PRINT MATTERS

These rates are ceilings. They're calculated net of existing tariffs, and every country has a list of exempt products. Several rates are also up for negotiation. Vietnam could drop to 20%, India to 17% and Singapore to 10% if they reach trade agreements. Your actual exposure depends on HTS codes, so look at the product annexes, not the headline numbers.

WHERE THERE'S NOWHERE TO HIDE

The usual escape routes are all on this list. Shifting production from China to Vietnam or Bangladesh doesn't save you much when every major Asian sourcing country is facing a similar rate. That changes the math on nearshoring, on dual sourcing, and on how much pricing power you really have.

THE TIMELINE

Written comments and requests to testify are due January 5, 2027. Public hearings start January 25. That means Fall 2027 costing is happening while the rules are still being written.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK

Pull your landed cost by country and by HTS code. Model your margins at the proposed rates and at the negotiated rates. Talk to your factories about splitting costs, and figure out which SKUs can carry a price increase and which ones can't. 

If one of these tariffs would really hurt your business, think about filing a comment. 

The brands that model this now will have choices. 

The ones that wait will just have to react.

Nvidia, Export Controls and the Battle for AI Infrastructure

There is an interesting development in the global AI race that deserves more attention, particularly from countries hoping to position themselves as the next destinations for AI infrastructure.

The Financial Times reports that Nvidia has instructed manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, to halt AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as they assess how to comply with new US export controls.

The restrictions, which took effect on 19 November 2026, require licences for certain advanced computing chips exported, re-exported or transferred within five designated countries: Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

There is another dimension to these controls. The US is also restricting the supply of large volumes of advanced computing capacity to companies headquartered in China, Macau and other designated jurisdictions, including where that computing capacity is accessed through overseas data centres. Existing data centres serving restricted customers have 90 days to seek authorisation.

The stated objective is understandable from Washington's perspective: prevent advanced American computing technology from reaching restricted Chinese entities through third-country infrastructure, cloud providers and data centres.

But I think the more interesting question is what this means for the future structure of the AI industry.

We often discuss the AI race as a contest between open-source and proprietary models. We debate who owns the models, who controls the algorithms and whether developers should be able to inspect, modify and redistribute the underlying technology.

However, there is another layer that receives considerably less attention: access to the computing infrastructure required to run these models.

You can download an open-weight model, have the technical expertise to modify it and even possess the legal right to deploy it. But none of that guarantees access to affordable GPUs on which to run it.

Similarly, a data-centre operator can invest billions in servers, establish facilities in a strategically located country and build relationships with regional customers, only to discover that supplying certain customers now requires authorisation from Washington.

This distinction matters because openness at the software and model layers does not necessarily translate into openness at the infrastructure layer.

And this is where I see a potentially significant structural consequence.

The new rules create different compliance burdens for different categories of operators. A large, well-capitalised cloud provider with established compliance departments, regulatory relationships and legal resources is considerably better positioned to navigate these restrictions than a smaller independent operator.

There is also an important asymmetry in the rules. Qualifying US-headquartered ultimate consignees or end users can benefit from an exception, subject to reporting requirements. Other regional operators do not enjoy the same general exemption.

My concern is not that these restrictions demonstrate a coordinated effort to favour proprietary AI providers. That would be a much bigger claim than the evidence supports.

Rather, it is that policies introduced for legitimate national-security reasons can have significant consequences for market concentration.

When access to computing becomes subject to increasingly complex licensing and compliance requirements, the advantage shifts towards organisations that already have the capital, scale and institutional relationships to navigate them.

In other words, we could end up with an AI ecosystem where the models are increasingly accessible, but the infrastructure required to run them remains concentrated in the hands of a relatively small number of powerful companies.

This is particularly relevant to countries like Kenya.

We should be careful about assuming that attracting foreign-owned data centres automatically translates into digital sovereignty. The physical location of computing infrastructure is only one part of the equation.

The more important questions are who owns the infrastructure, who determines access, which customers can use it, what happens when geopolitical restrictions change, and how much of the economic value remains in the local economy.

For Kenya, I would argue that the strategic priority should be building an ecosystem rather than simply attracting infrastructure investments.

That means exploring affordable shared GPU infrastructure, supporting independent local and regional cloud providers, developing the capacity to deploy open-weight models, maintaining access to alternative hardware and software ecosystems, establishing clear export-control compliance procedures and investing in local-language AI research.

It also means thinking beyond the immediate commercial opportunity of hosting foreign data centres.

The global AI contest is increasingly becoming a contest over the infrastructure that makes intelligence possible. And infrastructure, unlike software, is expensive to replicate and difficult to decentralise.

There is a lesson here from the history of the internet. Having access to the network did not automatically mean owning the infrastructure, controlling the platforms or capturing the economic value generated through it.

We should avoid making the same mistake with AI.

The ultimate question is not simply where the servers are located. It is who controls the computing capacity, who gets permission to use it and who captures the economic value that intelligence generates.

On November 19, Google confirmed that Android developer verification goes global in January 2027.

In simple terms: if your app is installed on a certified Android device, from Play or from anywhere else, the developer behind it needs a verified identity and a registered app. If not, a normal install gets blocked.

This isn't a test anymore. It has been live since September 30 in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand.

Here's what changes for teams that ship apps:

→ The rollout starts with seven app distributors: Google Play, Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo. Then it expands to every install source over several months.
→ Verification means a government ID and a $25 fee (per Ars Technica). Google says registering an app takes under ten minutes.
→ Students and hobbyists get free limited distribution accounts, now for up to 50 devices.
→ There are new APIs, so app registration can sit inside your CI pipeline.
→ Power users can still install unregistered apps through an "advanced flow", but it's buried behind warnings and a 24-hour wait.

The ones most likely to get caught out aren't big consumer apps on Play. They're the quiet ones:

→ Internal field-force or sales apps shared as an APK
→ Beta builds sent to clients outside Play
→ Kiosk, POS or event apps installed by hand
→ Apps on third-party stores where nobody owns the developer account anymore

If one of those stops installing next year, the fix itself is simple. Finding out the day users start getting blocked is the expensive part.

If we build or maintain an Android app with you at Yudiz, this is the question worth asking now: who owns the developer account, and is every package registered?

Does your team ship any Android app outside the Play Store?

THE FIRST GEOTHERMAL WELL MAY BEGIN IN ORBIT.

Deep beneath Indonesia's volcanic mountains lies an energy resource that satellites are helping exploration teams understand.

A geothermal prospect begins with a geological question.

Where is the heat coming from? Which underground structures allow hot fluids to circulate? And where should exploration capital be directed first?

In West Sumatra, a study published on 28 October 2026 offered a remarkable demonstration of how Earth observation can contribute to those decisions.

Researchers investigated the geothermal system around Mount Talang using two complementary sources of information.

The first wasLandsat-8 thermal imagery, providing spatial information about surface temperature and vegetation conditions.

The second was gravity-field data, which researchers modelled to investigate differences in the density of underground geological formations.

The result was a more detailed picture of the volcanic system.

Gravity anomalies highlighted zones associated with fractured and hydrothermally altered rocks.

The researchers identified a shallow alteration zone with a modelled density of approximately 2.30 g/cm³, together with a deeper intrusive body interpreted as a potential heat source.

Satellite thermal observations provided a complementary perspective on surface geothermal manifestations.

Together, the datasets helped connect visible surface conditions with geological structures beneath the mountain.

The commercial significance becomes clear when considering Indonesia's current geothermal expansion.

In August 2026, Pertamina Geothermal Energy (PGE) received a formal preliminary survey and exploration assignment for the Cubadak Panti area, also in West Sumatra.

The separate exploration area covers approximately 29,897 hectares, with preliminary geothermal resource potential estimated at 77 MWe.

Projects of this kind involve major decisions about geological surveys, exploration wells, development infrastructure and future electricity generation.

Each stage depends on increasingly detailed knowledge of the underground resource.

Satellite-derived thermal and gravity information offers a valuable starting point for regional screening, geological interpretation and exploration prioritisation.

For geothermal developers, the opportunity is to turn wide-area Earth observation into an increasingly sophisticated understanding of subsurface energy potential.

The next generation of exploration intelligence may combine thermal signatures, gravity anomalies and geological models into continuously improving spatial assessments of prospective geothermal fields.

The energy may be kilometres underground. The first useful clues can begin hundreds of kilometres above it.

26 Overseas Assignments. 11 Countries. More Than 16 Years. And Still Learning!

Every factory floor has something new to teach.

My current official assignment in Italy 🇮🇹 marks another chapter in a professional journey that began with my first overseas factory visit to China in 2010.

Over the years, these assignments have taken me across China, USA, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Malaysia, Poland, Indonesia, UAE, Nepal and now Italy — each offering a different perspective on manufacturing, technology and quality.

What makes this journey particularly interesting is the remarkable diversity of products and technologies encountered along the way.

From gas cylinders and cryogenic vessels to material-handling equipment, automotive tyres and tubes, engineering steels, automotive safety glass, footwear, aluminium packaging, insulated consumer products and wood-based products — every assignment has opened a different world of engineering.

The manufacturing processes have been equally fascinating — from traditional, skill-intensive operations to highly automated and robotic production systems involving forging, forming, machining, welding, heat treatment, rolling, coating, moulding, glass processing and assembly.

Testing has been another fascinating dimension. I have witnessed everything from conventional manual testing to sophisticated computer-controlled and robotic systems, covering mechanical, chemical, thermal, dimensional, pressure, endurance, impact and several other performance characteristics.

Perhaps the most interesting aspect has been seeing how different engineering disciplines come together on a single factory floor — mechanical and electrical engineering, metallurgy, materials science, polymers, chemistry, automation, measurement, product safety and quality assurance.

Yet, beyond the diversity of products, processes and technologies, one fundamental aspect remains common:

How the requirements of a standard translate into actual manufacturing practices, testing, quality control and ultimately, the finished product.

Equally valuable have been the interactions with engineers, technicians and quality professionals across different countries. Technologies, working practices and manufacturing environments may differ, but the commitment to quality, safety and reliability remains a common language.

These experiences have reinforced something I have come to appreciate over the years:

A standard may begin as a document, but its real journey begins when it reaches the factory floor.

After more than 16 years of overseas assignments, a new factory still feels a little like a new classroom.

Different countries. Different products. Different technologies. Different perspectives.

And always, something new to learn.

APAC's data centre boom has a delivery problem, not a capital problem.

The money is there. Hyperscalers, infrastructure funds and sovereign investors are committing billions across Singapore, Johor, Jakarta, Bangkok, Tokyo and Sydney. Land is being secured, power agreements are being negotiated, and AI demand is pushing capacity requirements higher than anyone forecast even two years ago.

What's much harder to secure is the people who can actually deliver it.

Building a mission-critical facility is nothing like a standard commercial project. You need project managers, cost managers, commissioning leads and site directors who understand power, cooling, redundancy and the unforgiving timelines hyperscale clients demand. That talent pool is small, and right now everyone is fishing in it at the same time.

A few things I'm seeing across the region:

1. Programmes are being won faster than delivery teams can be built. Developers are signing new campuses while their current projects are still short of senior site leadership.

2. The best people are being pulled in every direction. Developers, EPCs, consultancies and operators are all chasing the same experienced PMs, often for the same projects.

3. AI workloads are raising the bar. Higher rack densities and liquid cooling mean experience from five years ago doesn't always transfer, and people who've delivered AI-ready builds are in very short supply.

4. Clients want accountability, not headcount. Increasingly, they want partners who bring proven teams, clear ownership and a track record, rather than just bodies on site.

5. Local knowledge matters more than ever. Each market has its own regulations, power constraints and supply chain challenges, and teams who've delivered in one country can't always just switch to another.

The firms that win the next five years in APAC won't just be the ones with the strongest pipeline or the deepest pockets. They'll be the ones who can put the right people on site, quickly, and keep them there.

Capital builds the business case. People build the data centre.

Where are you seeing the biggest delivery gaps in the region right now: power, people or supply chain?
